title: ⭐⭐ Revision: the pairs, the marks and the past that is not a past

questions.prompt: Each of these four verbs marries one of the four complements, and only one. Put the pairs together.

options.text: make
maintain
overcome
take out
discipline
the rubbish
decisions
a difficulty

questions.explanation: make decisions is the English pair: whoever decides in a household makes the decisions. maintain discipline is the second: to maintain something is to keep it working, and discipline is exactly what has to be kept working day after day. overcome a difficulty is the third: to overcome is to get past an obstacle that stood in your way. take out the rubbish is the fourth, and it is the chore itself, the waste leaving the house. The four pairs cannot be swapped round, and no rule tells you why: nothing in the meaning of maintain announces discipline. That is the whole point of a collocation — it is learnt whole, verb and noun together, and never worked out from the parts.

questions.prompt: A pupil has copied a note from the board without a single mark: "her grandfather a tunisian sailor spent every winter in bizerte he taught his sons whole class to read a chart". Which version restores it?

options.text: Her grandfather, a Tunisian sailor, spent every winter in Bizerte. He taught his son's whole class to read a chart.
Her Grandfather, a Tunisian Sailor, spent every Winter in Bizerte. He taught his Son's whole Class to read a Chart.
Her grandfather a Tunisian sailor spent every winter in Bizerte, he taught his sons whole class to read a chart.
Her grandfather, a tunisian sailor, spent every winter in bizerte. He taught his son's whole class to read a chart.

questions.explanation: There are two sentences here, not one: the first stops after Bizerte and a full stop opens He. The phrase slipped between the subject and its verb is closed by a comma on each side, Tunisian keeps the capital of the country it is built on, Bizerte is a proper noun, and son's carries the apostrophe of possession. The version with no commas at all runs the description into the sentence and then joins two whole sentences with a comma, which English does not allow, and it drops the apostrophe as well. The version with a small t on tunisian and a small b on bizerte takes the capital off an adjective of nationality and off a town. The version with Grandfather, Sailor, Winter, Son's, Class and Chart treats six ordinary common nouns as names, and a season never takes a capital either.

questions.prompt: Fadhel asks his aunt: "Shall I bring the boxes on Friday?" She would prefer another day. Which answer does she give?

options.text: I'd rather you bring them on Saturday.
I'd rather you brought them on Saturday.
I'd rather you to bring them on Saturday.
I'd rather you will bring them on Saturday.

questions.explanation: would rather takes a past form as soon as the person who is to act is somebody other than the speaker, and that past is not about the past at all: the Saturday in question is still to come. "I'd rather you bring them on Saturday." leaves a present where that past form belongs. "I'd rather you to bring them on Saturday." copies the to of I'd prefer you to bring them, and would rather never takes one. "I'd rather you will bring them on Saturday." meets a future meaning with a future form, which is the natural guess and the wrong one: the structure is fixed, and it takes the past whatever day it is speaking about. When the speaker is the one who acts, no past and no subject: I'd rather stay at home.

questions.prompt: A pupil has written "have spent" in the gap of all four sentences of her homework. In which one is she right?

options.text: We ___ our holidays there in the summer of 2019.
We ___ our holidays there when we were still at school.
We ___ our holidays there two summers ago, with my aunt.
We ___ our holidays there ever since we got married.

questions.explanation: The present perfect needs a period that is still open, and ever since we got married gives exactly that: it starts at a point in the past and runs up to today, so the pupil is right in "We have spent our holidays there ever since we got married." in the summer of 2019 names a season that is over; two summers ago counts back to a moment that is closed; and when we were still at school shuts the whole thing inside a stretch of their lives that has ended. A named, finished time refuses the present perfect, and each of those three names one. Look also at the verb inside the since clause: got, a simple past. That is where the open period begins, and it never pulls the main verb back into the past with it.

questions.prompt: Two sentences are meant to say the same thing. The first is: "Some parents do not allow their children to have their own way." The second is built on let. Which second sentence is correct?

options.text: Some parents do not let their children have their own way.
Some parents do not let their children having their own way.
Some parents do not let their children to have their own way.
Some parents are not letting their children have their own way.

questions.explanation: let is followed by its object and then the bare verb, so allow their children to have becomes "let their children have": the change of verb costs you the to. "Some parents do not let their children to have their own way." carries that to over from allow, and it is the single most frequent mistake made with this verb. "Some parents do not let their children having their own way." puts an -ing form where the bare verb belongs. "Some parents are not letting their children have their own way." builds the structure correctly but changes the meaning: a continuous describes what is going on at the moment of speaking, while the first sentence states what some parents do in general.

questions.prompt: Yassine hired a minibus for the class trip, and it then turned out that the school's own bus had been free all along. Which comment on the wasted money is the English one?

options.text: You needn't hire a minibus.
You needn't had hired a minibus.
You needn't have hired a minibus.
You mustn't have hired a minibus.

questions.explanation: needn't followed by have and a past participle is the form kept for something that was done and turned out not to have been necessary, and the minibus was hired and paid for: "You needn't have hired a minibus." "You needn't hire a minibus." looks forward and says there is no need to hire one, which is advice arriving a week too late. "You needn't had hired a minibus." uses the wrong form of have: after a modal it stays in the base form, so have, never had. "You mustn't have hired a minibus." reaches for mustn't, which forbids: it would be an order not to hire one, and English does not use it to look back at money already spent for nothing.
